title: Right Side View of a Tree
statement:
A dashboard draws a binary tree of services, one level per row, and a narrow side panel shows only the node at the right end of each row. You must compute what the panel shows. Think of standing to the right of the tree and looking left: on each level you see the rightmost node, and it hides the others. A node in a left subtree is visible when nothing on the right reaches that level.

Trees use LeetCode's list format: tree[0] is the root, then the children of each node, left before right, level by level. None marks a missing child, and missing nodes list no children. Trailing Nones may be left off, and [] is the empty tree.

Write def solution(tree) that returns a list with one value per level, from the root's level down to the deepest level: the value of the rightmost node on that level. Return [] for the empty tree. Trees can be 10,000 levels deep, so avoid recursion.

examples.why: Levels are [1], [2, 3], [5, 4]. The last of each is 1, 3, 4.
Level 2 has only 4, a left-side node, and level 3 has only 5.

constraints: the tree can be 10,000 levels deep

think.q: Is the answer just the chain of right children from the root?
think.a: No. In [1, 2, 3, 4] the root's right child 3 has no children, but the left child 2 has a child 4 on the third level. Nothing on the right reaches that level, so you see 4. The answer is [1, 3, 4]. You need the last node of each level, whichever side it comes from.

think.q: Write the levels of [1, 2, 3, None, 5, None, 4] left to right, and take the last of each.
think.a: Level 0: 1. Level 1: 2, 3. Level 2: 5, 4 (5 is under 2, 4 is under 3). Last of each: 1, 3, 4.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: For each depth 0, 1, 2, ..., walk the whole tree again and keep the last node you meet at that depth when going left to right. That is one full walk per level, O(n * height), which is O(n^2) on a deep tree.

Breadth-first search, one level at a time. A queue holds exactly one level. Read its size, pop that many nodes (pushing their children left then right), and the last node you pop is the rightmost on that level. Each node goes through the queue once.

1. Build the tree. If it is empty, return [].
  2. queue = deque([root]), view = [].
  3. While the queue is not empty: size = len(queue); pop size nodes, pushing each node's left child then right child.
  4. Append the value of the last node popped in that round.
  5. Return view.

The empty tree. A single node. A tree that only goes left (every node is visible). A left subtree deeper than the right one. Equal values on a level (you return values, so duplicates are fine). A 10,000-deep tree: BFS uses no recursion, so it is safe.

hints: The rightmost node of a level is not always a right child. Try [1, 2, 3, 4].
Process the tree level by level with a queue. At the start of a level, len(queue) is exactly the number of nodes on it.
Push children left before right. Then the last node you pop on each level is the one you see from the right.
brute:
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def build(tree):
    # LeetCode list -> linked nodes. Each popped parent takes the next two slots.
    if not tree or tree[0] is None:
        return None
    root = Node(tree[0])
    queue = deque([root])
    i = 1
    while queue and i < len(tree):
        node = queue.popleft()
        if i < len(tree) and tree[i] is not None:
            node.left = Node(tree[i])
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(tree) and tree[i] is not None:
            node.right = Node(tree[i])
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root

def solution(tree):
    # For each depth, walk the whole tree left to right and keep the last node
    # at that depth. One walk per level: O(n * height).
    root = build(tree)
    view = []
    depth = 0
    while root is not None:
        last = None
        stack = [(root, 0)]
        while stack:
            node, d = stack.pop()
            if d == depth:
                last = node            # later in left-to-right order wins
                continue
            for child in (node.right, node.left):   # pop left first
                if child is not None:
                    stack.append((child, d + 1))
        if last is None:
            break
        view.append(last.val)
        depth += 1
    return view
explain:
Example 2, [1, 2, 3, 4, None, None, None, 5]: 1 has children 2 and 3; 2 has a left child 4; 4 has a left child 5.

  • Level 0: the queue is [1]. Pop 1, push 2 and 3. The last pop is 1.
  • Level 1: the queue is [2, 3]. Pop 2 (push 4), pop 3. The last pop is 3.
  • Level 2: the queue is [4]. Pop 4, push 5. The last pop is 4, a left-side node, because 3 has no children.
  • Level 3: the queue is [5]. The last pop is 5. The answer is [1, 3, 4, 5].

Reading the size at the start of each round is what separates levels: children pushed during the round belong to the next level and are not popped yet. Every node is pushed and popped once, so the time is O(n). A DFS that visits the right child first and records the first node at each new depth also works, but it needs an explicit stack here.
complexity: O(n) time, O(width) extra space for the queue
